title: C++: an object on the stack and one on the heap

steps.note: Entering `main` reserves room in its **stack frame** for `rex` (a whole Dog: a string and an int) and for `pip` (just an address). Nothing is initialised yet.
`Dog rex("Rex", 3);` calls the **constructor** on that stack space. `this` points at rex. The **member initialiser list** `: name_(name), age_(age)` initialises the members before the body runs.
`new Dog(...)` allocates a Dog on the **heap**, runs the constructor there, and returns its **address**. `pip` stores that address (a pointer).
`rex.bark()` - the compiler knows rex is a Dog, so it calls `Dog::bark` directly, passing `&rex` as the hidden `this` parameter.
steps.out:
constructed Rex
constructed Pip
Rex says woof

steps.note: `delete pip;` runs the destructor and **frees** the heap memory. `pip` still holds the old address - a **dangling pointer**. Using it now would be undefined behaviour. (Modern C++ uses `std::unique_ptr` so this can't be forgotten.)
steps.out:
constructed Rex
constructed Pip
Rex says woof

steps.note: When `main` returns, its frame is popped and **rex is destroyed automatically**. Stack objects need no `delete`. That's the basis of RAII.
steps.out:
constructed Rex
constructed Pip
Rex says woof
